Medication adherence.summary: Adherence to prescribed treatment and lifestyle advice is crucial to prevent recurrent cardiovascular (CV) events after acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Adherence is sub-optimal, ranging ~50% in primary prevention to ~66% in secondary prevention. An estimated 9% of ASCVD events in Europe result from sub-optimal medication adherence.
contributors_to_nonadherence: lack of patient-centred care and disease acceptance
recommendations: Use polypills where appropriate to improve adherence
Adopt patient-centred care, education of health professionals, and patient-reported outcomes
Address psychological drivers of adherence with a whole-systems approach

Polypill (SECURE study).summary: The SECURE randomized controlled trial tested a polypill strategy (containing aspirin, ramipril, and atorvastatin) versus usual care in elderly ACS patients.
Polypill (SECURE study).outcomes: Polypill strategy was associated with a significant reduction in major CV events, driven by a 33% reduction in CV mortality.
Polypill (SECURE study).implication: Polypills that combine guideline‑recommended secondary prevention drugs can increase adherence and may improve hard outcomes.

Use of technology.summary: Mobile phone applications and mobile health (mHealth) tools are being explored to improve medication adherence.
Use of technology.evidence: Promising but clinical trials of sufficient size and duration are still needed.
Use of technology.recommendation: Consider technology-enabled adherence supports while awaiting stronger trial evidence.

Lifestyle management.summary: Lifestyle management is a cornerstone of comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation (CR). Evidence for beneficial effects on prognosis largely comes from primary prevention, but secondary prevention studies indicate similar benefits.
Lifestyle management.recommendation: Promote healthy lifestyle behaviors as part of secondary prevention and CR.

Tobacco.summary: Tobacco abstinence after ACS is associated with reduced risk of re-infarction (approx. 30–40%) and death (approx. 35–45%).
interventions: Begin smoking cessation interventions during hospitalization combining behavioural interventions, pharmacotherapy, and counselling
Use very brief advice and evidence-based dialogue during encounters
Consider drug interventions with behavioural support

notes: All forms of NRT are effective
Bupropion aids long-term cessation with similar efficacy to NRT
Varenicline is the most effective medical treatment to support smoking cessation and is considered safe to use in ACS patients

other_points.relapse_risk: Many patients continue or resume smoking after ACS, especially those with depression or environmental exposures
other_points.expected_weight_change: Average weight gain of ~5 kg can be expected after quitting smoking
